explanations.answer: Run with endurance the race set out for them
explanations.explanation: The writer says it plainly: "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) Notice the word endurance. That's the kind of running he has in mind, friend. And he says it with a great cloud of witnesses all around.

explanations.answer: Sit back and watch the faithful go first
explanations.explanation: I like the comfy chair idea, but the writer doesn't hand out seats. He says "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) The cloud of witnesses surrounds us, and we're the ones told to run.

explanations.answer: Build a monument to remember the faithful
explanations.explanation: The writer never mentions a monument. After pointing to the great cloud of witnesses, he says "…let us run with endurance the race set out for us." (Hebrews 12:1) The faithful surround us, and we're told to get moving. I would also have no idea where to put a statue in my bakery.

explanations.answer: The sin that so easily entangles
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer says to throw off "…every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles…" (Hebrews 12:1) Entangles is a great word. I have personally lost a fight with a mixer cord, so I know how a tangle goes.

explanations.answer: The fear that so easily discourages
explanations.explanation: Fear sounds like a fair guess, but it's not the word the writer uses. He says to throw off "…every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles…" (Hebrews 12:1) The thing that tangles you up is sin. Toss it off, friend.

explanations.answer: The pride that so easily deceives
explanations.explanation: Pride is a fair guess, but the text doesn't say it here. The writer says to throw off "…every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles…" (Hebrews 12:1) Sin is what he names. Sin is the thing that wraps around your feet.

Jesus is who the writer points to: "Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith…" (Hebrews 12:2) A runner who keeps looking around gets wobbly. Fix your eyes, friend, and keep them on Him.

Moses, Israel's leader, is one of the faithful people in Hebrews 11 (Hebrews 11:23-29). But the writer says to fix our eyes on Jesus, "…the author and perfecter of our faith…" (Hebrews 12:2) Moses isn't named in this verse. The eyes go to Jesus.

Abraham is one of the faithful in Hebrews 11 (Hebrews 11:8-19), so it's a fair thought. But the writer tells us to fix our eyes on Jesus, "…the author and perfecter of our faith…" (Hebrews 12:2) Abraham isn't named in this verse. Jesus is where the eyes go.

explanations.answer: For the joy set before Him
explanations.explanation: Right. The writer says Jesus, "…for the joy set before Him endured the cross…" (Hebrews 12:2) Joy was set before Him, and He endured. After that, He sat down at the right hand of God's throne.

explanations.answer: To prove His strength to sinners
explanations.explanation: The writer doesn't give that reason. He says Jesus, "…for the joy set before Him endured the cross…" (Hebrews 12:2) The reason the text gives is joy. I'd stick with what it says.

explanations.answer: To win the praise of the crowd
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about praise. It says Jesus, "…for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame…" (Hebrews 12:2) Scorning the shame is the opposite of chasing applause. The reason given is the joy set before Him.
True. The writer says Jesus "…endured the cross, scorning its shame…" (Hebrews 12:2) The shame was real, and He scorned it. Then He sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
This one is true, friend. The writer says Jesus "…endured the cross, scorning its shame…" (Hebrews 12:2) So the text really does say it. The shame was there, and He scorned it.

explanations.answer: At the right hand of the throne of God
explanations.explanation: Yes. The writer says Jesus "…sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." (Hebrews 12:2) The cross came first. Then came the seat at God's right hand.

David was Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), so I see the thought. But the writer says Jesus "…sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." (Hebrews 12:2) The throne in this verse is God's. Jerusalem isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: Beside Moses on the holy mountain
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a great name, but he isn't in this verse. The writer says Jesus "…sat down at the right hand of the throne of God." (Hebrews 12:2) There's no mountain here, just the throne of God. Jesus is the One in focus.

Weary is the word. We're told to consider Jesus "…so that you will not grow weary and lose heart." (Hebrews 12:3) You know weary: four snoozes in and the bed still wins. Looking at Jesus is the writer's cure.

Proud is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't use it. It says to consider Him "…so that you will not grow weary and lose heart." (Hebrews 12:3) Weary pairs with lose heart. Both are about running out of steam.

Careless is not in this verse. The writer says to consider Him "…so that you will not grow weary and lose heart." (Hebrews 12:3) The danger here is getting worn out. And the answer is to look at Jesus.

Not quite, friend. The writer says, "In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood." (Hebrews 12:4) So it's the opposite of what the card said. The word to notice is yet.

Right, it's false. The text says, "In your struggle against sin, you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood." (Hebrews 12:4) Those readers had not gotten to that point. The coach is making a point, and the point is to keep going.
That's it. The exhortation says, "My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord…" (Hebrews 12:5) Don't shrug it off, friend. It's worth listening to.
That actually flips it around. The exhortation says, "…do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord…" (Hebrews 12:5) Taking it lightly is the thing to avoid. So the son should take it seriously.

The exhortation doesn't say to ignore it. It says, "…do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you." (Hebrews 12:5) Pay attention, and don't lose heart either. That's two things to hold onto.
Yes. The exhortation says, "For the Lord disciplines the one He loves…" (Hebrews 12:6) It goes on to say, "…He chastises every son He receives." Discipline and love show up together in this verse.

The verse says nothing about rejection. It says, "For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives." (Hebrews 12:6) The one disciplined is the one He loves. And He receives that son.

explanations.answer: The one who is a stranger to Him
explanations.explanation: Strangers aren't mentioned in this verse. It says, "For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives." (Hebrews 12:6) The verse speaks of the one He loves and every son He receives.

Father is the word. The writer asks, "For what son is not disciplined by his father?" (Hebrews 12:7) Right before that, he says that God is treating you as sons. It's a father and son picture all the way through.

A teacher is a reasonable guess, but it's not what the verse says. The writer asks, "For what son is not disciplined by his father?" (Hebrews 12:7) It's a father and son picture. The writer says God is treating you as sons.

Master doesn't appear here. The writer asks, "For what son is not disciplined by his father?" (Hebrews 12:7) It's about sons and a father. And the line just before it says God is treating you as sons.

It's actually the other way around, friend. The writer says, "If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons." (Hebrews 12:8) So going without discipline doesn't mark a true son. The text says the opposite.

Right, it's false. The writer says, "If you do not experience discipline like everyone else, then you are illegitimate children and not true sons." (Hebrews 12:8) So a child with no discipline isn't called a true son. Discipline is part of how God treats His sons.

explanations.answer: Submit to Him much more and live
explanations.explanation: That's right. The writer asks, "Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9) Much more, friend. We respected earthly fathers, and this is the Father of our spirits.

explanations.answer: Respect Him about the same amount
explanations.explanation: The writer raises the bar. He asks, "Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9) Much more, not about the same. And the verse ends with live.

explanations.answer: Keep a careful distance from Him
explanations.explanation: That's not what the writer says. He asks, "Should we not much more submit to the Father of our spirits and live?" (Hebrews 12:9) The verse speaks of submitting, and of living.

Holiness is the word. The writer says God disciplines us "…for our good, so that we may share in His holiness." (Hebrews 12:10) Earthly fathers disciplined us for a short time as they thought best, and God does it for our good. If you left my idea of good up to me, it would be extra cookie dough, so I'm glad the aim here is holiness.

Wealth is a tempting guess, but the verse doesn't say it. The writer says God disciplines us "…for our good, so that we may share in His holiness." (Hebrews 12:10) The goal is holiness. It isn't money.
Power isn't in this verse. The writer says God disciplines us "…for our good, so that we may share in His holiness." (Hebrews 12:10) What we share in is His holiness. That's the good he names.

Peace is the word. The writer says discipline "…yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it." (Hebrews 12:11) Notice that it comes later on. It's a harvest, and harvests take time.

Riches would be nice, but the verse says something else. Discipline "…yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it." (Hebrews 12:11) Just before that, the writer says no discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. So what you get for the pain is righteousness and peace, not a paycheck.

Fame isn't what the writer has in mind. He says discipline "…yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it." (Hebrews 12:11) The harvest is righteousness and peace. Nobody's asking for autographs.

You got it, baker. The writer says, "Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees." (Hebrews 12:12) That Therefore points back to the verse before it. Discipline seems painful at the time, but later it yields "…a harvest of righteousness and peace…" to those who have been trained by it. So when the pain makes you feel limp and weak, the writer says to strengthen up and keep going, because the training pays off later.
Rest sounds so nice, doesn't it? But the writer says, "Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees." (Hebrews 12:12) The instruction is to strengthen them. Keep going, friend.
Stuffing your limp hands in your pockets won't help. The writer says, "Therefore strengthen your limp hands and weak knees." (Hebrews 12:12) Nobody's told to hide anything. Strengthen them.
True. The writer says, "Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed." (Hebrews 12:13) That's the exact line. The goal is healing.

This one is true, friend. The writer says, "Make straight paths for your feet, so that the lame may not be disabled, but rather healed." (Hebrews 12:13) So the card matched the text. The hope in the verse is healing.
